strengths: The paper addresses an important evaluation problem in brain-to-text decoding: distinguishing generalization across subjects from generalization to unseen linguistic stimuli. This is directly relevant to interpreting NLP performance on cognitive signals.

The experiments cover two modalities, two public datasets, and two established decoding architectures. The large reported differences across splitting protocols motivate closer scrutiny of evaluation practices; four seeds are included for the leakage-rate analysis.

The intended joint subject-and-stimulus holdout is appropriate for the stated transfer setting. The graph formulation provides an intuitive starting point, recognizes overlapping fMRI windows, and explicitly acknowledges the cost of discarding data.
weaknesses: The central causal claims are not established by Section 4.4. Decreasing validation reconstruction loss does not demonstrate encoder degradation, and improving BLEU with longer training does not prove decoder memorization. Random encoder initialization does not remove information from brain signals, and comparisons also change learning rates and training budgets. Matched experiments with shuffled or removed signals and language-only controls are needed to support claims that generation largely ignores cognitive input.

The proposed algorithms do not guarantee the advertised separation as written. Algorithm 1, line 15, restores edges without excluding stimuli assigned to validation/test; Algorithm 2, line 33, restores edges without excluding held-out subjects. These operations can reintroduce overlap into initially disjoint splits. Algorithm 1 also iterates over subjects, contradicting Section 3.3's instruction to select one edge per stimulus. Corrected pseudocode and explicit checks of pairwise disjointness are necessary.

The leakage metrics and reported results contain substantive inconsistencies. Equation (7) measures an intersection of identical recordings rather than shared subject identity and has a zero denominator for subjects absent from training. In Table 3, UniCoRN at 80 epochs under method (c) has ROUGE-1 F=84.64, P=63.16, and R=71.50. These values are incompatible with standard F1 computation or consistent averaging: mean F1 cannot exceed (P+R)/2=67.33. The definitions and results require reconciliation.

Performance differences across protocols conflate overlap with other changes. The proposed method discards observations and changes subject and stimulus distributions, but retained sample counts and matched-data comparisons are absent. Consequently, the performance drop cannot be attributed quantitatively to contamination alone. Downstream results also lack uncertainty estimates across subject/task partitions and training seeds, particularly concerning with only 12 ZuCo participants.

The scope of the contamination claim is overstated. Holding out both subjects and stimuli is appropriate for the authors' chosen objective, but subject overlap is not inherently leakage in a study targeting calibrated, within-subject decoding of unseen text. The paper should distinguish valid evaluation targets before characterizing existing protocols as contaminated.

Reproducibility is insufficient for the claimed benchmark release. Although some hyperparameters and preprocessing references are supplied, the manuscript provides no benchmark/code access link, exact split assignments, post-filtering and post-discard counts, or clear inference and checkpoint-selection protocols. These omissions, together with the algorithmic and empirical issues above, prevent a sound Findings recommendation. Corrected specifications and controlled re-evaluation could support resubmission next cycle.
